title: 出版社に断られて  (Turned Down by Publishers)

segments.t: Inside a Sapporo publishing office, Toru Muranishi pitches a bold new book idea to a cautious editor. After getting turned away at the door, Muranishi climbs back into the car with Toshi and refuses to slow down. Listen first for the contrast between Muranishi's polite pitch and the editor's blunt refusal.
うちで出す？
お願いします、本気で本を作りたいんです。
自分が言ってること、本当に分かってる？
これ見てください。
いや、ここは日本だよ。
こんな本を出したら犯罪になっちゃうよ。
とにかく、うちではやれない。
さあ、帰った、帰った。
池沢に会ってからおかしいぞ。
そりゃ断るわな。
次だ。
北海道中の会社、回る気かよ？
The editor brushes Muranishi off in casual office speech, while Toshi groans from the driver's seat. Let's walk through the key lines.
うちで出す？

'Publish it at our company?' "Uchi" literally means home or inside, and in business Japanese it doubles as 'our company' or 'our shop'. Paired with "de", at, and "dasu", to put out or publish, a rising tone turns two words into an incredulous question.
お願いします、本気で本を作りたいんです。

'Please, I seriously want to make this book.' Opening with "onegaishimasu" makes a respectful plea before asking a favor. "Honki de" means in earnest—literally 'true spirit'—and "tsukuritai" attaches "tai", want to, onto "tsukuru", to make.
自分が言ってること、本当に分かってる？

'Do you really understand what you are saying?' "Jibun" points back to 'yourself', while "hontou ni" asks 'really' or 'truly'. Casual speech trims "itte iru" and "wakatte iru" down to "itteru" and "wakatteru", dropping the "i" sound at natural speed.
これ見てください。
'Please look at this.' "Kore" is 'this thing right here' in my hand. Spoken Japanese often drops the object marker before "mite kudasai", the everyday polite way to say 'please look'.
いや、ここは日本だよ。

'No, this is Japan.' Softening his pushback with "iya", no or well, the editor points to "koko", right here. "Nihon da yo" finishes with "yo" to remind Muranishi of an obvious fact he seems to be ignoring.
こんな本を出したら犯罪になっちゃうよ。

'If we publish a book like this, it will become a crime.' "Dashitara" builds 'if we publish' from "dasu", to put out. At the end, "natchau" squeezes "natte shimau"—ending up in an unwanted state—around "hanzai", crime.
とにかく、うちではやれない。

'Anyway, we cannot do it at our company.' "Tonikaku" sweeps the debate aside with 'anyway' or 'in any case'. "Yarenai" is the 'cannot do' cousin of "yaru", to do, preceded by "uchi de wa" to stress 'not at our place'.
さあ、帰った、帰った。
'Come on, off you go, go home.' Curiously, Japanese can bark a brisk shooing command by repeating "kaetta", which looks like 'went home', as if your departure is already settled.
池沢に会ってからおかしいぞ。

'You have been acting strange ever since meeting Ikezawa.' Putting "atte kara" after a person names the starting point: 'ever since meeting'. "Okashii" covers both funny and strange, and rough "zo" adds a blunt, man-to-man punch.
次だ。
'On to the next one.' Two syllables do all the work: "tsugi", next, plus firm "da". You will hear "tsugi" everywhere in Japan, from train station announcements to shop lines.
北海道中の会社、回る気かよ？

'Are you planning to visit every company across Hokkaido?' Adding "juu" onto "Hokkaidou" stretches the meaning across the whole island, so "Hokkaidou-juu no kaisha" means companies all over Hokkaido. Ending with "mawaru ki ka yo" asks 'do you seriously intend to go around them all?' Now let's hear the whole publishing-office scene again without interruption.
うちで出す？
お願いします、本気で本を作りたいんです。
自分が言ってること、本当に分かってる？
これ見てください。
いや、ここは日本だよ。
こんな本を出したら犯罪になっちゃうよ。
とにかく、うちではやれない。
さあ、帰った、帰った。
池沢に会ってからおかしいぞ。
そりゃ断るわな。
次だ。
北海道中の会社、回る気かよ？
Keep "uchi" in mind whenever Japanese speakers talk about their own home, shop, or company, and listen for how "tsugi"—next—packs a whole change of plan into one brisk word. Until next time.
また会いましょう。
